hero.subtitle: Open Shortest Path First - the dominant interior gateway routing protocol

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state routing protocol designed for IP networks. It is an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) that distributes routing information between routers within a single Autonomous System (AS).

OSPF is the most widely deployed IGP in enterprise networks. It uses Dijkstra's Shortest Path First algorithm to compute the best path to each destination, hence its name.

Link-State Protocol
Each router maintains a complete topological database of the network and independently calculates routing tables.
Convergence
OSPF converges rapidly after network changes through immediate flooding of Link State Advertisements (LSAs).
Hierarchical Design
Networks can be divided into areas to reduce routing overhead and contain LSA flooding.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
OSPF operates by flooding link-state advertisements (LSAs) throughout the routing domain. Each router constructs a link-state database (LSDB) representing the complete network topology, then runs the SPF algorithm to build a shortest-path tree rooted at itself.

sections.title: Areas
sections.content:
OSPF uses a two-level hierarchy with a backbone area (Area 0) and non-backbone areas. All inter-area traffic must transit the backbone, providing a hub-and-spoke topology that simplifies routing.

Area 0 (Backbone)Central area through which all inter-area traffic flows
Standard AreaAccepts all LSA types; full routing information
Stub AreaNo external routes; uses default route to exit the area
Totally StubbyNo external or inter-area routes; only a default route
NSSANot-So-Stubby Area: allows limited external route injection via Type 7 LSA

Area Border Routers (ABRs) connect areas to the backbone and summarize routing information between them, reducing the size of each area's link-state database.

sections.title: LSA Types
sections.content:
Link State Advertisements are the fundamental units of information in OSPF. Each LSA type serves a specific purpose in the routing topology.

Type 1Router LSA - Describes a router's links within an area
Type 2Network LSA - Generated by DR for multi-access segments
Type 3Summary LSA - Inter-area route advertisements by ABRs
Type 4ASBR Summary - Describes route to an ASBR
Type 5AS External LSA - External routes redistributed into OSPF
Type 7NSSA External - External routes in NSSA areas

sections.title: SPF Algorithm
sections.content:
The Shortest Path First algorithm (Dijkstra's algorithm) is the core computation of OSPF. Each router independently runs SPF to build a shortest-path tree rooted at itself, then derives its routing table from this tree.

Step 1: Initialize
Place the root (self) on the candidate list with cost 0. All other nodes start at infinity.
Step 2: Select Best
Move the candidate with lowest cost to the SPF tree. This node's shortest path is now known.
Step 3: Update Neighbors
For each neighbor of the newly added node, update its cost if the path through this node is shorter.
Step 4: Repeat
Continue until all reachable nodes are on the SPF tree. The routing table is derived from the tree.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
OSPF routers discover neighbors by exchanging Hello packets at regular intervals. The Hello protocol establishes and maintains neighbor relationships and elects Designated Routers on multi-access networks.

Hello IntervalTime between Hello packets (typically 10 seconds)Configurable
Dead IntervalTime to declare a neighbor down (typically 40 seconds)4x Hello
DR ElectionRouter with highest priority (or Router ID) becomes DRPer segment
BDRBackup Designated Router provides redundancyPer segment

Neighbors must agree on Hello interval, Dead interval, area ID, and authentication to form an adjacency. Mismatched parameters are a common cause of OSPF adjacency failures.
